title: Episode 67: The Lost State of Franklin: America's Forgotten 14th State
description:
The Lost State of Franklin: America's Forgotten 14th State: How mountain settlers in East Tennessee seceded from North Carolina, created their own constitution, and bartered whiskey and raccoon pelts for taxes. Join Rebecca and George for an immersive historical deep dive into this extraordinary chapter of the American story.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. In the turbulent years immediately following the American Revolutionary War, before the United States Constitution was drafted, the western frontier was a cauldron of rebellion and survival. In 1784, pioneering settlers living in the Appalachian valleys of what is now East Tennessee felt abandoned by their mother state of North Carolina. Facing Native American raids and possessing no military protection, currency, or courts, they did the unthinkable: they declared independence and founded their own sovereign American republic. Named in honor of Benjamin Franklin, the State of Franklin elected its own governor, signed treaties, fought rival militias, and collected taxes in whiskey, beaver furs, and raccoon pelts. George brings us the colorful, forgotten history of America's lost fourteenth state.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: ABANDONED ON THE WATAUGA
In the seventeen seventies and seventeen eighties, the lush river valleys of the Watauga, Holston, and Nolichucky rivers in the southern Appalachian mountains were settled by fiercely independent frontiersmen: Scots-Irish pioneers, former long hunters, and veteran Revolutionary War riflemen. These settlers, living across the rugged Blue Ridge Mountains, legally fell within the western territorial boundaries of the state of North Carolina. But North Carolina was bankrupt from the Revolutionary War, crushed under heavy continental debt. In June seventeen eighty-four, the North Carolina legislature took an extraordinary step: to avoid paying its share of federal war debt, the state ceded its entire western territory—twenty-nine million acres stretching from the mountains to the Mississippi River—to the weak national government under the Articles of Confederation. The Appalachian settlers were stunned. North Carolina had essentially abandoned them overnight without consulting their consent, leaving nearly thirty thousand pioneers stranded in the wilderness without legal government, civil courts, land registry offices, or military protection against hostile Cherokee and Creek warriors who defended their ancestral hunting grounds. Frontier families lived in fortified log stations along the rivers, clearing dense cane brakes and defending their hearths against Native raids without a single shilling of assistance from North Carolina. The dramatic events unfolded against a backdrop of deep cultural transformation, as rural communities confronted the rapid onset of modern industrial technology and national media attention. Frontier settlers living along the Watauga and Holston rivers had established their own democratic compact years earlier, forging a fierce tradition of self-governance in the rugged valleys of the western Appalachian wilderness.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE BIRTH OF FRANKLIN
Furious at North Carolina's betrayal, delegates from Washington, Sullivan, and Greene counties convened in the log settlement of Jonesborough in August seventeen eighty-four. Led by the charismatic frontier soldier Colonel John Sevier—revered across the frontier as 'Nolichucky Jack' for his heroic leadership at the pivotal Battle of Kings Mountain—the settlers resolved to organize their own independent state. In December seventeen eighty-four, they drafted a provisional constitution, establishing an independent commonwealth originally proposed as 'Frankland'—the land of the free. Seeking national legitimacy and federal protection, they quickly renamed the new sovereign territory the 'State of Franklin' in honor of America's beloved elder statesman, Benjamin Franklin. The delegates dispatched letters to Dr. Franklin in Philadelphia, begging for his endorsement and political advice. Franklin wrote back with polite diplomatic praise, encouraging their independence while advising them to seek a peaceful, legal reconciliation with the national Congress. Benjamin Franklin was flattered by the homage, writing warm diplomatic letters to Sevier praising the rugged independence and democratic spirit of the mountain pioneers. Eyewitness accounts recorded in local diaries and regional newspapers captured the tension and uncertainty of the moment, preserving vivid details for future generations of historians. John Sevier was a legendary Indian fighter and Revolutionary War hero of the Battle of Kings Mountain, whose charisma and frontier courage commanded the unswerving loyalty of riflemen across eastern Tennessee.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: NOLICHUCKY JACK TAKES THE HELM
In March seventeen eighty-five, the General Assembly of the State of Franklin convened in Greeneville, which was chosen as the permanent capital. The legislature elected John Sevier as their first and only governor, established a bicameral legislature, created county courts, and organized an official state militia. Governor Sevier was the epitome of the frontier hero: handsome, daring, and possessing an extraordinary bond with his mountain riflemen, he had fought in dozens of desperate battles against British loyalists and Native war parties. Sevier moved with executive energy: negotiating treaties with Cherokee chiefs at Dumplin Creek to open hundreds of thousands of acres for homestead settlement, surveying township boundaries, and appointing tax collectors and county sheriffs. In May seventeen eighty-five, Franklin memorialized the Continental Congress in New York, seeking formal admission as the fourteenth state of the American Union. Seven states voted in favor of admitting Franklin, but under the Articles of Confederation, a two-thirds majority of nine states was required. The bid failed by just two votes, leaving Franklin an unrecognized, sovereign border republic. Governor Sevier rode through the mountain settlements on horseback, rallying his militia with fiery orations that appealed to their Revolutionary heritage of self-government and freedom. Cocke carried a petition signed by hundreds of frontier settlers to the Continental Congress in New York, arguing eloquently that frontier communities deserved the full constitutional protections of American statehood.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: TAXES IN RACCOON PELTS AND WHISKEY
One of the most extraordinary aspects of the State of Franklin was its economic system. The frontier republic suffered from an absolute, chronic shortage of minted gold, silver, or paper currency. Spanish silver dollars and continental scrip rarely reached the mountains. To solve the liquidity crisis, the Franklin General Assembly passed a landmark fiscal statute in seventeen eighty-five establishing an official barter currency. All state salaries, taxes, judicial fees, and commercial transactions were legally payable in verified frontier commodities at fixed statutory rates. A gallon of rye whiskey was valued at two shillings and sixpence; an unblemished beaver pelt was worth six shillings; a deer skin was three shillings; a bushel of bacon was two shillings; and a prime otter skin was five shillings. Most famous of all was the raccoon skin: officially valued at one shilling and three pence, raccoon pelts were legally stamped by county clerks and circulated like dollar bills. Legends arose of clever mountain counterfeiters who sewed raccoon tails onto common possum skins to deceive unsuspecting tax collectors. County clerks meticulously stamped each raccoon skin with black ink on the tail, creating a unique frontier currency that circulated through general stores and tavern ledgers across the mountains. The currency shortage in Franklin was so severe that taxes were legally payable in raccoon skins, bacon, whiskey, and tobacco, with counterfeiting of animal skins becoming a common frontier legal offense.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE DUAL GOVERNMENTS ON THE BORDER
The State of Franklin's independence was fiercely contested by North Carolina. Recognizing that western lands were valuable for future speculation, North Carolina rescinded its cession act and demanded that the mountain counties submit to Raleigh's authority. Governor Richard Caswell of North Carolina offered pardons and tax exemptions to any settler who rejected Sevier's government. This created a chaotic, surreal state of affairs in East Tennessee: two competing governments operating simultaneously in the same counties. In towns like Jonesborough, there was a Franklin county court and a North Carolina county court; a Franklin sheriff and a North Carolina sheriff; and two competing sets of tax collectors trying to seize the same livestock. Neighbor turned against neighbor. When a North Carolina court convened, Franklin militia raided the courthouse, seized the court dockets, and threw the magistrate into the mud; days later, North Carolina loyalists retaliated by breaking into Franklin offices and stealing their records. Competing magistrates frequently held rival court sessions across the street from one another, with rival posses arresting each other deputies in a chaotic spectacle of frontier legal warfare. The armed standoff highlighted the bitter factional divisions tearing the frontier community apart, as neighbors who had fought side by side against British redcoats now leveled rifles at one another over competing legal loyalties.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE BATTLE OF FRANKLIN
The conflict erupted into open military bloodshed in February seventeen eighty-eight. Colonel John Tipton, the staunch leader of the pro-North Carolina faction, obtained a court writ from North Carolina and raided Governor John Sevier's plantation, seizing several of Sevier's horses and cattle to satisfy delinquent North Carolina taxes. Tipton took the livestock to his fortified log homestead near Johnson City. An enraged Governor Sevier mobilized one hundred and fifty Franklin riflemen and marched on Tipton's farm, surrounding the log house in a blinding winter blizzard. Sevier brought a small bronze cannon and demanded Tipton's unconditional surrender. For three days, the Franklin forces besieged the homestead, exchanging rifle fire in the snow. On the morning of February twenty-ninth, a relief column of North Carolina militia under Major George Maxwell surprised Sevier's lines from the rear. In the swirling snowstorm, a brief, chaotic gun battle erupted: three men were killed, several were wounded, and Sevier's forces were routed. The 'Battle of Franklin' shattered the military power of the republic. The snow-covered clearing around the Tipton farm became a battleground where neighbors who had fought together at Kings Mountain traded musket fire in the freezing Appalachian wind. The courage and resilience demonstrated by everyday citizens during this critical trial inspired observers across the country, showing that ordinary people can rise to meet extraordinary challenges. Sevier's dramatic rescue by heavily armed loyalists demonstrated that the rugged mountain settlers viewed Nolichucky Jack as their true leader, regardless of official warrants issued by distant state officials in Raleigh.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE ASHES OF FRANKLIN AND THE BIRTH OF TENNESSEE
Following his military defeat, John Sevier was briefly arrested for high treason by North Carolina authorities, but was dramatically rescued from jail by loyal mountain riflemen who rode into the courtroom with cocked revolvers. Recognizing that Franklin was doomed and that the new United States Constitution of seventeen eighty-seven provided federal stability, Sevier took the oath of allegiance to North Carolina in seventeen eighty-nine. North Carolina formally ceded its western lands to the new federal government, which organized the region into the Southwest Territory. In seventeen ninety-six, the territory was admitted to the Union as the sixteenth state: Tennessee. In a stunning political resurrection, the mountain people overwhelmingly elected John Sevier as the very first Governor of the state of Tennessee, serving six terms with distinction. Today, the State of Franklin remains an unforgettable American legend: a four-year sovereign frontier republic where pioneer courage, mountain independence, and raccoon pelt currency proved that the American spirit of self-determination would always forge its own destiny in the wilderness. The spirit of the Lost State of Franklin laid the institutional foundation for Tennessee, demonstrating that American democracy drew its deepest strength not from royal charters, but from the consent of free people in the wilderness. Today, historic markers and museum collections honor these legendary figures, reminding us that the spirit of American adventure and perseverance continues to guide our shared journey forward. Though the State of Franklin dissolved after four turbulent years, its spirit of frontier independence laid the bedrock for Tennessee's admission to the Union in seventeen ninety-six, with John Sevier proudly serving as the new state's first governor.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Lost State of Franklin was a daring experiment in frontier democracy that paved the way for Tennessee statehood. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week as we journey to Alabama for the heroic story of the Tuskegee Airmen.
